beats.text: Can your fingernail cover the giant Moon?
beats.visual_intent: frame 0: giant moon over rooftops, a finger rising beside it

beats.text: Yes. At arm's length, it covers the same amount of Moon, low or high.
beats.visual_intent: fingernail covers the low moon, then the high moon

beats.text: So the giant Moon isn't really giant.
beats.visual_intent: giant moon deflates to normal size

beats.text: Photos with the same settings show the same width near the horizon and high up.
beats.visual_intent: two photo frames side by side, equal moons, ruler

beats.text: And down low, the Moon is actually about 1.5 percent farther away.
beats.visual_intent: night scene: arrow from viewer to low moon is longer

beats.text: The leading idea: your brain thinks the horizon Moon is far away, so it sees it bigger.
beats.visual_intent: brain with a magnifier pointed at the horizon

beats.text: Scientists still argue about the exact cause.
But you can shrink it yourself: look through a rolled-up paper tube.
beats.visual_intent: paper tube aimed at the moon, moon shrinks inside the circle

beats.text: Or check it with your fingernail. Save this for the next big Moon.
beats.visual_intent: back to the giant moon and the finger

title_options: The giant horizon Moon isn't bigger
Shrink the giant Moon with a paper tube
publish.description: Same-setting photos show the horizon Moon the same width as the high Moon; it is even about 1.5 percent farther away. The size comes from your brain.

cta.decision_reason: the video ends on a test viewers can only do on a moonrise night; saving it is the useful next step
cta.spoken: Save this for the next big Moon.

beats.text: Can your fingernail cover the giant Moon?
beats.visual_intent: frame 0: giant moon over rooftops, a finger rising beside it

beats.text: It can, at the horizon and overhead.
beats.visual_intent: fingernail covers the low moon and the high moon

beats.text: Because the Moon doesn't grow. Same-setting photos show the same width.
beats.visual_intent: two photo frames, equal moons, ruler

beats.text: It's even about 1.5 percent farther away when it's low.
beats.visual_intent: night scene: longer arrow to the low moon

beats.text: Your brain does the growing. It judges the horizon Moon as farther off, so it sees it bigger.
beats.visual_intent: brain with a magnifier aimed at the horizon

beats.text: Around 1960, Lloyd Kaufman and Irvin Rock found support for that idea.
beats.visual_intent: two researchers with a notebook and a check mark

beats.text: Try a paper tube, and the giant Moon shrinks.
beats.visual_intent: paper tube aimed at the moon, small moon in the circle

beats.text: So next time it looks huge, reach for your fingernail.
beats.visual_intent: back to the giant moon and the finger

title_options: Why the horizon Moon looks bigger
Your brain makes the Moon look bigger
publish.description: The horizon Moon is not bigger: photos show the same width, and it is about 1.5 percent farther away. A paper tube makes the illusion shrink.
